abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Spinal cord aging is a critical physiological process that compromises central nervous system (CNS) homeostasis and plasticity. Exercise, as a systemic intervention with broad health benefits, has been shown to delay neurodegeneration and preserve tissue function; however, its impact on dynamic cellular lineage evolution and intercellular communication within the aging spinal cord remains poorly characterized. In this study, we employed single‐nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA‐seq) to construct a high‐resolution cellular atlas of the mouse spinal cord under young, aged, and aerobic exercise‐intervened conditions. By integrating unsupervised clustering, cell proportion analysis, pseudotime trajectory reconstruction, gene regulatory network (GRN) inference, and intercellular communication mapping, we systematically characterized transcriptional and cellular alterations associated with aging and their modulation through exercise. Aging induced pronounced shifts in cell‐type composition and subpopulation structures, which were partially reversed by exercise intervention. Pseudotime analyses of oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, and microglia revealed that exercise remodeled their differentiation trajectories and restored functional states associated with myelin formation, metabolic homeostasis, and inflammation control. GRN analysis identified several key regulators whose centrality and expression were disrupted during aging but reestablished after exercise, suggesting a recovery of transcriptional network organization. Furthermore, intercellular communication analysis revealed reduced signaling strength and connectivity during aging, particularly within gap junction pathways, which were partially restored by exercise, indicating improved cellular coordination. Together, these findings provide a comprehensive single‐cell landscape of the aging spinal cord and demonstrate that exercise reprograms cellular lineages and regulatory networks, offering mechanistic insights into how it mitigates CNS aging and preserves neural function.

sec.p: Keywords: aerobic exercise, single‐nucleus RNA sequencing, spinal cord aging

abstract.p: Aerobic exercise remodels the aged murine spinal cord at single‐cell resolution. snRNA‐seq reveals that aging induces pronounced shifts in cell‐type composition and subpopulation structure, whereas exercise partially reverses these changes by remodeling oligodendrocyte, astrocyte, and microglial differentiation trajectories and functional states, restoring gene regulatory networks, and rewiring intercellular communication networks. These findings provide a cellular and molecular framework for exercise‐induced rejuvenation of the aging spinal cord.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: As a vital component of the central nervous system (CNS), the spinal cord undergoes progressive functional decline with aging [1]. This complex process involves alterations in cellular composition, disruption of myelin homeostasis, and reduced synaptic plasticity, along with remodeling of the immune microenvironment, dysregulation of intercellular communication networks, and reprogramming of gene regulatory circuits [2, 3, 4]. Functional deterioration of the spinal cord has been closely associated with impaired motor coordination, reduced neural control efficiency, and increased susceptibility to neurodegenerative disorders [5, 6, 7]. However, the dynamic features of multicellular state transitions and their underlying molecular mechanisms during spinal cord aging remain poorly understood. In particular, high‐resolution characterization of lineage‐specific differentiation and temporal transcriptional programs at the single‐cell level is still lacking.

Exercise is a well‐established, non‐pharmacological systemic intervention known to confer wide‐ranging physiological benefits, including the maintenance of homeostasis across neural, muscular, immune, and metabolic systems [8, 9, 10]. Large‐scale consortia such as the Molecular Transducers of Physical Activity Consortium (MoTrPac) are systematically mapping multi‐tissue molecular responses to exercise, further validating its systemic impact [11]. Within the CNS, exercise has been shown to enhance neuronal function and plasticity, while modulating the structure and activity of non‐neuronal components, increasing local regenerative capacity, and promoting neuroimmune interactions [10, 12, 13]. Although extensive research has examined the brain's response to exercise, it remains unclear whether the aging spinal cord exhibits comparable plasticity. Specifically, an integrative understanding of exercise‐induced changes in cellular states, gene regulatory networks, and intercellular signaling within the spinal cord remains limited.

In this study, we employed single‐nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA‐seq) to construct a comprehensive cellular and transcriptional atlas of the spinal cord from young, aged, and aerobic exercise‐intervened mice. By focusing on the remodeling of cellular lineage trajectories, transcriptional regulatory networks, and intercellular communication structures, we identified age‐associated shifts in transcriptional states and local signaling perturbations, along with candidate pathways and molecular targets modulated by exercise. Our findings demonstrate that exercise intervention exerts multidimensional corrective effects on aging‐associated cellular activation patterns and functional decline, revealing distinct anti‐aging transcriptional signatures. These results not only enhance our understanding of spinal cord aging but also provide theoretical foundations and molecular clues for developing targeted strategies to mitigate spinal cord dysfunction.

sec.title: Animals
sec.p: Male C57BL/6J mice were purchased from Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Co. Ltd. (Beijing, China). Animals were housed in a temperature‐controlled environment (22°C ± 2°C) with 50%–60% humidity under a 12 h light/dark cycle, with free access to standard chow and water. Mice were allowed to acclimate for 1 week before the start of experiments. Based on age, animals were divided into young (2 months old, n = 6) and aged (18 months old, n = 6) groups. Each age group was further randomly assigned to either a control or aerobic exercise intervention, resulting in four groups in total: Young‐Control (YC, n = 3), Young‐Exercise (YE, n = 3), Aged‐Control (AC, n = 3), and Aged‐Exercise (AE, n = 3). All experimental procedures were approved by the Ethics Committee of Beijing Sport University and conducted in accordance with institutional guidelines for animal care and use (No. 2024049A).

sec.title: Exercise Training Protocol
sec.p: Following 1 week of adaptive feeding, mice in the exercise groups underwent an aerobic treadmill training program. To determine the appropriate training intensity, the maximal oxygen consumption (VO2max) of each mouse was assessed using an incremental treadmill running test. The aerobic exercise program was then initiated at 60% VO2max, corresponding to moderate‐intensity training. Mice in the exercise groups performed treadmill running 5 days per week, 50 min per session, for 8 consecutive weeks. To account for improvements in aerobic capacity, VO2max was reassessed every 2 weeks, and running speeds were adjusted accordingly to maintain the relative intensity. Control group mice were placed on a stationary treadmill for the same duration to control for environmental exposure. Gentle electric stimuli were applied when necessary to encourage continuous running in the exercise groups.

sec.title: Tissue Collection and Processing
sec.p: All mice were sacrificed 24 h after the final exercise session to minimize the acute effects of exercise and capture steady‐state transcriptional changes. Animals were deeply anesthetized with isoflurane until loss of reflexes was confirmed. Following anesthesia, spinal cord segments T8–T10 were rapidly dissected on ice to ensure tissue integrity. Fresh tissues were snap‐frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80°C for RNA extraction and sequencing.

sec.title: snRNA‐Seq
sec.p: Frozen spinal cord tissues were mechanically homogenized on ice, followed by lysis using Nuclei Lysis Buffer for 5 min with gentle mixing. The lysate was filtered through a 40 μm cell strainer to remove tissue debris. The filtrate was centrifuged at 500 × g for 5 min to pellet nuclei, which were then resuspended in PBS containing 1% BSA and RNase inhibitor. After a second filtration step, the purified nuclear suspension was obtained. Nuclear transcriptome libraries were constructed using the 10× Genomics Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3′ v3.1 platform, following the manufacturer's instructions. Each sample aimed to capture approximately 6000–10 000 nuclei. cDNA synthesis, amplification, and library preparation were conducted using the 10× Genomics system, and library quality was assessed using an Agilent Bioanalyzer. Sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform (n = 1 biological replicate per group).

sec.title: Preprocessing and Quality Control of the snRNA‐Seq Data
sec.p: Raw sequencing data were processed using Cell Ranger software (v6.1.2, 10× Genomics), including FASTQ alignment to the mouse reference genome (mm10) and generation of gene expression matrices using the cellranger count module. Each sample was processed independently. Downstream analysis was conducted using the Seurat package (v5.0.0) [14]. Low‐quality nuclei were filtered by retaining those with ≥ 200 detected genes and < 5% mitochondrial gene content. Potential doublets were predicted and removed using the DoubletFinder package (v2.0.5) [15]. High‐quality nuclei were normalized using the SCTransform method, with batch effects regressed out. Sample integration was performed using the PrepSCTIntegration and FindIntegrationAnchors functions.

The integrated dataset was subjected to dimensionality reduction using principal component analysis (PCA), followed by t‐distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t‐SNE) based on the top 20 principal components. Clustering was performed using FindNeighbors and FindClusters (resolution = 1.2). Marker genes for each cluster were identified using FindAllMarkers, with significance thresholds of adjusted p < 0.05 and log2 fold change > 0.5. Identified marker genes were compared with the CellMarker 2.0 database and classic marker references for cell type annotation [16].

sec.title: Differential Expression Analysis
sec.p: Differential expression analysis was performed using Seurat's FindMarkers function with the Wilcoxon rank‐sum test. Pairwise comparisons were conducted between Young‐Control vs. Young‐Exercise, Aged‐Control vs. Aged‐Exercise, and Young‐Control vs. Aged‐Control. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified based on an adjusted p < 0.05 (Bonferroni correction) and an absolute log2 fold change > 0.35. All comparisons were performed at the cell type level to ensure specificity and avoid artifacts from compositional changes.

sec.title: Gene Ontology (GO) Analysis
sec.p: Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis was conducted using the Metascape online tool (https://metascape.org), focusing on the GO‐Biological Process (BP) category [17]. Default parameters were used for enrichment calculations. Significantly enriched terms were defined by a false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05. Cytoscape software (v3.9.1) was used to visualize functional networks based on Metascape‐exported structures, facilitating interpretation of core biological modules [18].

sec.title: Differential Gene Regulatory Network Analysis
sec.p: Gene regulatory network (GRN) analysis was performed using the bigScale2.0 package for Oligodendrocytes, Astrocytes, and Microglial cells [19]. Comparisons focused on Young‐Control vs. Aged‐Control and Aged‐Control vs. Aged‐Exercise. For each cell type under each condition, GRNs were inferred using the compute. Network function. To ensure comparable network density, the homogenize. Networks function was applied. Centrality metrics, including degree, betweenness, closeness, and rank, were computed using compare. Centrality to assess the relative regulatory importance of genes across conditions.

sec.title: Pseudotime Analysis
sec.p: Pseudotime trajectory analysis was conducted using the Monocle2 package (v2.34.0) on Oligodendrocytes, Astrocytes, and Microglial cells [20]. To ensure comparability across groups and computational efficiency, each group was downsampled to 1200 cells per cell type. Highly variable genes were identified using dispersionTable, and cells were ordered in pseudotime based on these genes. Dimensionality reduction was performed using the DDRTree algorithm (v0.1.5), and developmental trajectories were visualized in two dimensions. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) along the pseudotime trajectory were identified using differentialGeneTest, and the top 1000 DEGs (ranked by q‐value) were retained for further analysis and visualization using the ClusterGVis package (v0.1.2).

sec.title: RNA Extraction, Reverse Transcription, and Quantitative PCR (qPCR)
sec.p: Total RNA was isolated from snap‐frozen spinal cord tissue samples using TRIzol reagent (Thermo Fisher) according to the manufacturer's instructions. RNA concentration and purity were determined spectrophotometrically. First‐strand cDNA was synthesized from 1 μg of total RNA using a reverse transcription kit (Thermo Fisher). Quantitative PCR was performed on a real‐time PCR system (ABI 7500, Thermo Fisher) using SYBR Green chemistry (PowerUp SYBR Green Master Mix, Thermo Fisher) in a 20 μL reaction volume. Cycling conditions were 95°C for 2 min followed by 40 cycles of 95°C for 15 s and 60°C for 30 s, with melt‐curve analysis to verify specificity. Relative expression was calculated by the 2^−ΔΔCt method using Actb as internal controls. Primer sequences are provided in Table S1.

sec.title: Cell–Cell Communication Analysis
sec.p: Cell–cell communication analysis was performed using the CellChat package (v2.1.2) on Young‐Control, Aged‐Control, and Aged‐Exercise samples [21]. Following the official CellChat workflow, CellChat objects were constructed for each sample, and differentially expressed ligands and receptors were identified at the cell subtype level. Interaction probabilities between cell types were computed based on the law of mass action. Statistical significance was evaluated using permutation tests (p < 0.05). Signaling networks were constructed for each group, and outgoing/incoming signaling patterns were analyzed to identify dominant senders and receivers. Centrality analysis was conducted to determine core signaling sources and targets.

To evaluate functional similarities in signaling across conditions, joint manifold learning was applied to the signaling networks from different groups. Euclidean distances within the learned manifold were used to identify signaling pathways with the most altered functional similarity between Young‐Control vs. Aged‐Control and Aged‐Control vs. Aged‐Exercise. Finally, information flow (i.e., the summed interaction strength across all cell‐type pairs) was calculated to quantify the overall activity of each signaling pathway and identify conserved or oppositely regulated pathways.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: All data processing and statistical analyses were conducted using R software (v4.4.3, R Development Core Team, Vienna, Austria). Differential expression analysis was performed using the Wilcoxon rank‐sum test with Bonferroni correction. GO enrichment analysis used the hypergeometric test with FDR‐adjusted p‐values. Significance of cell–cell communication interactions was assessed using permutation testing. Unless otherwise specified, all statistical tests were two‐tailed, and statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05.

sec.title: Single‐Nucleus RNA Sequencing Reveals Dynamic Remodeling of Spinal Cord Cell Composition During Aging and Aerobic Exercise
sec.p: To systematically characterize the impact of exercise intervention on spinal cord cell composition and states across different ages, we performed single‐nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA‐seq) analysis on spinal cord tissues from four groups of mice. A total of 37 403 high‐quality nuclei were obtained for downstream analyses. Based on the expression of cell type‐specific marker genes, we identified 11 major cell types using t‐SNE dimensionality reduction and clustering (Figure 1A), which were broadly categorized into three groups (1), neural lineage cells, including neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), and microglia (2), vascular‐associated cells, including endothelial cells and pericytes; and (3), supportive and structural cells, including fibroblasts, ependymal cells, and Schwann cells. Clear differences in cell distribution among groups were observed in the t‐SNE space (Figure 1B). Further analysis of the relative proportions of each cell type across groups (Figure 1D), revealed that oligodendrocyte proportions decreased after exercise intervention (in both young and aged mice), whereas the proportions of neurons and astrocytes generally increased, suggesting that exercise may enhance neural support and neuronal functional activity. Proportions of microglia, Schwann cells, and fibroblasts were elevated in aged control mice but were reduced to near‐young levels after exercise, indicating that exercise may alleviate aging‐associated inflammatory responses and fibrotic tendencies. Conversely, OPCs were significantly reduced in aged mice but markedly increased after exercise, implying a role for exercise in maintaining oligodendrocyte precursor cell homeostasis. The expression patterns of cell type‐specific marker genes showed clear stratification (Figure 1C, left panel of 1E). Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis indicated that marker genes of each cell type were mainly involved in biological processes consistent with their known functions (Figure 1E, right panel), such as myelination for oligodendrocytes, lipid metabolism and epithelial regulation for astrocytes, neural development and neurotransmission modulation for neurons, and innate immune responses, inflammatory regulation, and Toll‐like receptor signaling for microglia. These functional enrichments further confirmed the robustness of our cell annotations and provided a basis for subsequent analyses focusing on specific cell subsets.

sec.title: Age‐Dependent and Cell Type‐Specific Transcriptional Responses to Aerobic Exercise
sec.p: To investigate the molecular effects of exercise at different ages, we identified differentially expressed genes (DEGs) by comparing the young exercise (YE) and aged exercise (AE) groups with their respective controls (YC and AC; Table S2). The AE group exhibited a markedly greater number of DEGs than the YE group (Figure 2A), suggesting a more pronounced transcriptional response to exercise in aged mice. Mapping YE‐specific, AE‐specific, and shared (common) DEGs to different cell types revealed that DEGs were predominantly enriched in neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes (Figure 2B–E). Functional enrichment analysis showed that YE‐specific DEGs were mainly involved in synaptic structure regulation, membrane protein localization, cell projection morphogenesis, and catalytic activity regulation, highlighting the exercise‐responsive structural and functional plasticity of young neural tissue. In contrast, AE‐specific DEGs were significantly enriched in pathways related to oxidative phosphorylation, cytoskeletal remodeling, synaptic vesicle transport, membrane potential regulation, and cognition‐associated processes (Figure 2I,J), suggesting that exercise in aged mice primarily drives metabolic activation and synaptic remodeling. Common DEGs were enriched in biological processes including mitochondrial function (such as mitochondrial translation and respiratory chain complex assembly), ion homeostasis, oxidative stress response, neural development, and synapse organization (Figure 2K). These highly conserved processes likely represent core mechanisms of the exercise response shared across age groups.

(B–C) Distribution of YE‐specific and AE‐specific DEGs across cell types by number (B) and percentage (C). (D–E) Number (D) and proportion (E) of shared DEGs (common DEGs) across cell types, reflecting conserved exercise responses. (F) Venn diagram identifying “rescue DEGs” as the intersection between aged‐control (AC vs. YC) and exercise group (AC vs. AE) DEGs. (G–H) Quantification (G) and proportion (H) of rescue DEGs per cell type. (I–J) GO enrichment networks for YE‐ and AE‐specific DEGs (I), with enrichment levels across groups (J). (K) GO network analysis of common DEGs, highlighting shared exercise‐responsive pathways. (L) GO enrichment of rescue DEGs reveals functions in cell structure, signaling, and tissue remodeling.

sec.p: We next examined whether exercise could rescue aging‐associated molecular changes. DEGs were compared between the aged control (AC) and aged exercise (AE) groups, defining “Rescue DEGs” as genes showing opposite expression trends between these comparisons (i.e., upregulated in AC vs. YC but downregulated in AC vs. AE, and vice versa; Table S2). A total of 135 candidate Rescue DEGs were identified (Figure 2F; Table S3). Cell‐type mapping revealed that these genes were mainly enriched in neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and microglia (Figure 2G,H). Notably, microglia, endothelial cells, and Schwann cells contributed more prominently to DEGs in AC vs. YC, whereas neurons, OPCs, and pericytes contributed more to those in AC vs. AE. GO enrichment of Rescue DEGs highlighted processes such as cell size regulation, extracellular matrix organization, O‐glycosylation, tyrosine phosphorylation, endothelial cell proliferation, synaptic plasticity, and skeletal system development (Figure 2L). These findings indicate that exercise reprograms multiple dimensions of spinal cord cellular functionality during aging and may restore developmental and plasticity‐related programs.

sec.title: Pseudotime Analysis of Oligodendrocytes Reveals Aerobic Exercise‐Mediated Remodeling of Aging‐Associated Transcriptional Dynamics
sec.p: We further performed lineage reconstruction analysis on the oligodendrocyte population. Unsupervised clustering divided these cells into three subpopulations: C1, C2, and C3 (Figure 3A). C1 showed high expression of marker genes such as Pdgfra and Cspg4, indicative of OPCs; both C2 and C3 expressed mature oligodendrocyte markers including Mog, Plp1, Mbp, Mag, and Mal. Additionally, C3 uniquely expressed Adgrv1 and 9330111N05Rik, suggesting a regionally or functionally specialized mature subtype (Figure 3B). Consistent with this, the C1 (OPC) population expanded after exercise, while the proportion of the C3 mature subtype decreased, with C2 remaining relatively stable (Figure 3C). We reconstructed the dynamic differentiation trajectory of oligodendrocytes using pseudotime analysis (Figure 3D,E). The analysis positioned C1 at the early stage of the trajectory, with C2 and C3 occupying the middle‐to‐late stages (Figure 3F), consistent with the developmental progression from OPCs to mature oligodendrocytes. We identified the top 1000 differentially expressed genes along the trajectory and grouped them into four dynamic expression modules (Clusters 1–4) (Figure 3G). Cluster 1 and Cluster 2 genes were highly expressed at early pseudotime points and were enriched in functions such as synapse structure regulation and glial differentiation, reflecting active signaling during the OPC stage. Cluster 3 showed a gradual upregulation pattern, with genes involved in membrane localization and small GTPase signaling pathways, likely related to myelin formation processes. Cluster 4 genes peaked in the later stages, associated with motor behavior and presynaptic structure regulation, possibly representing mature oligodendrocyte‐mediated functional integration.

sec.p: To further explore transcriptional regulatory network (GRN) changes across groups, we applied the bigScale2 algorithm to construct GRNs for oligodendrocyte lineages in each group and performed differential regulatory network (DRN) analysis. Specifically, we compared aged control (AC) versus young control (YC) groups to identify genes whose centralities were significantly altered by aging, and then compared aged exercise (AE) versus aged control (AC) groups to identify genes whose centralities were modulated by exercise. Genes showing opposite centrality changes in these two comparisons were considered candidate markers of exercise‐mediated “rescue” effects, yielding 536 candidates (Figure 3H). Finally, by integrating three independent criteria (1), the top 1000 pseudotime‐dynamic genes (2), DEGs rescued by exercise, and (3), genes with reversed GRN centrality changes restricted to transcription factors, ligands, and receptors—we identified 11 potential key regulators (Figure 3I): Nlgn1, Negr1, Ebf1, Thrb, Tsc22d1, Sema5a, Cntn1, Dscam, Hivep2, Zmiz1, and Adgrb1. Pseudotime mapping revealed that these genes were predominantly expressed at early differentiation stages corresponding to the OPC subpopulation (Figure 3J), suggesting that their dysregulation may contribute to aging‐associated remyelination blockades. To experimentally validate these findings, we performed qPCR analyses in YC, AC, and AE groups (Figure 3K). Ten genes displayed significantly reduced expression in AC compared with YC, whereas their levels were markedly restored in AE. In contrast Hivep2 expression was elevated in AC but significantly suppressed by exercise in AE. Together, these results highlight a set of candidate regulators positioned at the OPC stage that may underlie impaired oligodendrocyte differentiation during aging and its partial restoration through exercise.

sec.title: Lineage Reconstruction of Astrocytes Reveals Aerobic Exercise‐Regulated State Transitions During Aging
sec.p: Unsupervised clustering of astrocytes identified two major subpopulations (Figure 4A). Cluster C1 exhibited high expression of classical reactive astrocyte markers, including Gfap and Aqp4, suggesting an activated or stress‐responsive phenotype. In contrast, Cluster C2 was characterized by elevated expression of Gpc5 and Trpm3, previously linked to neurotrophic or homeostatic supportive astrocyte states [22] (Figure 4B). Comparative analysis revealed an increased proportion of C1 cells and a marked reduction of C2 cells in the aged exercise group relative to aged controls (Figure 4C), indicating that exercise may reshape the astrocytic state composition. To investigate the potential lineage relationship between these two astrocyte subtypes, we constructed pseudotime trajectories (Figure 4D,E), which revealed a continuous transition axis from C1 to C2. C1 cells were primarily located at the root of the trajectory, whereas C2 cells were enriched at the terminal branches (Figure 4F). Differential expression analysis along pseudotime identified the top 1000 dynamically regulated genes, which were subsequently grouped into five clusters with distinct expression patterns (Figure 4G). These clusters indicated a sequential transition encompassing cytoskeletal remodeling, ion homeostasis, enhanced cell adhesion, reduced metabolic activity, and gradual disengagement from neuronal regulatory functions. Specifically, genes in Clusters 1 and 2 gradually increased along the trajectory and were enriched in cytoskeleton organization, gliogenesis, and calcium ion homeostasis, reflecting early‐stage morphological maturation. Cluster 3 genes peaked during the early to middle stages and were associated with cell adhesion and synaptic assembly, suggesting enhanced connectivity with surrounding neural networks. In contrast, the expression of genes in Clusters 4 and 5 declined along the trajectory; the former was associated with metabolic transport, while the latter was linked to the negative regulation of neurite outgrowth and neuronal apoptosis, suggesting diminished metabolic and regulatory support as astrocytes progressed toward a mature or reactive state.

sec.p: At the transcriptional regulatory level, gene regulatory networks (GRNs) were constructed for each group using the bigScale2 algorithm, followed by differential regulatory network (DRN) analysis. Comparison of gene centrality changes between the aged controls (AC) vs. young controls (YC) and AC vs. aged exercise (AE) contrasts identified 98 genes exhibiting opposite trends, defined as “rescue genes” (Figure 4H). These genes may represent transcriptional nodes perturbed during aging and restored by exercise. By integrating pseudotime‐dynamic genes, differentially expressed rescue genes, and GRN centrality‐reversed nodes restricted to transcription factors, ligands, and receptors, we identified three candidate key regulators (Figure 4I). Gli2 and Gtf2ird1 were mainly expressed in the early stages of the astrocyte trajectory, suggesting roles in maintaining or initiating supportive states, whereas Glis3 was enriched in later stages, indicating an association with reactive astrocytic phenotypes (Figure 4J). Consistent with these observations, qPCR validation showed that Gli2, Glis3, and Gtf2ird1 expression levels were significantly elevated in AC compared with YC, whereas their expression was markedly reduced in the AE group, confirming the restorative effects of exercise on astrocytic regulatory programs (Figure 4K).

sec.title: Lineage Analysis of Microglia Reveals Aerobic Exercise‐Mediated Modulation of Aging‐Associated Activation Programs
sec.p: Unsupervised clustering of microglia identified two distinct functional subtypes (Figure 5A). Cluster C1 expressed Tmem119 and Siglech, characteristic of homeostatic microglia, whereas Cluster C2 showed elevated expression of Sall1 and Apoe, the latter being upregulated during aging and neuroinflammatory conditions, indicative of an activated or stress‐responsive phenotype (Figure 5B). In aged controls, the proportion of C1 cells significantly increased, suggesting an aging‐associated activation trend. Although exercise slightly reduced this proportion in aged mice, it remained higher than in young controls, indicating a partial suppressive effect on microglial activation (Figure 5C). In contrast, young‐exercise and young‐control groups displayed comparable subpopulation structures, suggesting limited effects of exercise on microglial heterogeneity under non‐pathological conditions. Pseudotime trajectory analysis revealed a transition path from C2 (homeostatic) to C1 (activated), with C2 cells concentrated at the root and C1 cells at the terminal (Figure 5D–F), delineating a progressive transition from quiescence to activation. Clustering of the top 1000 differentially expressed genes along pseudotime identified six major transcriptional modules (Figure 5G). Cluster 1 genes were markedly upregulated at the terminal phase and enriched in “positive regulation of interleukin‐1 production,” indicating a classical pro‐inflammatory state. Clusters 2 and 3 showed intermediate‐to‐late upregulation and were involved in tissue remodeling, cell–matrix adhesion, wound healing, and morphological regulation, potentially reflecting transitional stages toward full activation. In contrast, Cluster 4 genes were stably expressed during early and mid‐pseudotime but declined toward the end, and were associated with dendritic development and monocyte migration, possibly reflecting dynamic migratory and morphological transitions. Clusters 5 and 6 exhibited continuous downregulation and were enriched in pathways regulating cell positioning, calcium ion homeostasis, small GTPase signaling, and cytoskeleton organization, indicating a progressive decline in structural stability and homeostatic capacity during aging.

(J) Expression pattern of Plp1 across pseudotime, colored by subcluster. (K) Quantitative PCR validation of the microglial regulator Plp1. Expression was significantly elevated in aged controls (AC) compared with young controls (YC), and exercise intervention in aged mice (AE) suppressed this increase. Data are presented as mean ± SD, and statistical significance was determined using one‐way ANOVA with post hoc tests. **p < 0.01.

sec.p: Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) were constructed and compared across groups using centrality analysis, revealing one key rescue gene whose network centrality was significantly restored by exercise in aged mice (Figure 5H). By integrating pseudotime‐dynamic genes, differential expression changes, and GRN centrality reversal restricted to transcription factors, ligands, and receptors, we identified Plp1 as the sole core regulator meeting all criteria (Figure 5I). Along the pseudotime trajectory, Plp1 was highly expressed in homeostatic microglia and progressively declined as cells transitioned toward activated states (Figure 5J). qPCR validation further confirmed that Plp1 expression was significantly elevated in aged controls (AC) compared with young controls (YC), whereas exercise intervention markedly suppressed its expression in aged mice, reinforcing the role of Plp1 as a potential exercise‐responsive regulator of microglial activation (Figure 5K).

sec.title: Cell–Cell Communication Analysis Reveals Aerobic Exercise‐Induced Rewiring of Signaling Networks in the Aged Spinal Cord
sec.p: To further investigate how aging and exercise affect intercellular communication in the spinal cord, we performed ligand–receptor‐based inference to compare cell–cell signaling networks among young controls (YC), aged controls (AC), and aged‐exercise (AE) mice. Aging significantly reduced both the number of interactions (Figure 6A) and overall communication strength (Figure 6B), whereas exercise restored interaction frequency but not signal intensity, suggesting that exercise enhanced communication frequency but only partially recovered signaling efficiency. At the cellular level, communication among multiple spinal cord cell types was generally weakened with aging. Notably, interactions between microglia and endothelial cells, Schwann cells, OPCs, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes were paradoxically increased in AC mice, suggesting compensatory enhancement within immune–glial networks under impaired global signaling (Figure 6C). Furthermore, fibroblasts exhibited distinct rewiring of their signaling patterns in aged mice, showing increased communication with OPCs and reduced interactions with ependymal cells, potentially reflecting shifts in repair targets or instability within the stem cell niche. Interestingly, neuron–OPC bidirectional communication decreased in number but increased in strength in aged mice (Figure 6D). This included autocrine neuron–neuron and OPC–OPC signaling, as well as paracrine neuron–OPC and OPC–neuron pathways. These changes suggest a shift from widespread but sparse signaling to more concentrated and intense interactions, possibly reflecting altered regulatory dynamics within the aging niche.

caption.p: Exercise partially restores age‐impaired cell–cell communication, with GAP signaling as a key remodeled pathway. (A) Bar plot showing the total number of ligand–receptor interactions across cell subtypes in YC, AC, and AE groups. (B) Total communication strength per group, defined as the sum of all inferred interaction probabilities. (C) Heatmap displaying changes in the number of interactions between cell types; red: Increased, blue: Decreased. Top and side bar plots show net input/output changes. (D) Heatmap of interaction strength alterations across cell types; colors denote direction and magnitude of change. (E–G) Bubble plots of incoming/outgoing signals among cell types in YC (E), AC (F), and AE (G); dot size represents communication volume. (H) Joint manifold learning‐based integration of intercellular signaling networks across groups, with clustering based on sender–receiver functional similarity. (I–J) Top 20 signaling pathways with the greatest Euclidean distance in joint manifold space between YC vs. AC (I) and AC vs. AE (J), indicating major functional rewiring. (K–M) Network centrality analysis of GAP signaling across YC (K), AC (L), and AE (M), identifying key sender, receiver, mediator, and influencer cell types. (N–P) GAP pathway communication networks in each group. Nodes represent cell types; edge width is proportional to predicted interaction probability.

sec.p: Spatial mapping of cell subpopulations in two‐dimensional signaling space revealed marked positional shifts, particularly among neurons and OPCs (Figure 6E–G), highlighting the plasticity of intercellular communication states in response to aging and exercise. To identify key signaling pathways involved in state transitions, we applied joint manifold learning to integrate communication networks across the three groups and clustered pathways based on sender–receiver functional similarity (Figure 6H). The GTPase‐activating protein (GAP) pathway exhibited the greatest similarity shifts across both aging and exercise transitions (Figure 6I,J), implicating it as a central mediator of age‐related network perturbation and exercise‐induced remodeling. Network centrality analysis further confirmed that the topological structure of the GAP signaling pathway was profoundly altered with aging. In AC mice, fibroblasts lost nearly all functional roles as senders, receivers, influencers, and mediators. These functions were markedly restored in AE mice, approaching levels observed in young controls (Figure 6K–M). Specifically, fibroblast communication with pericytes, ependymal cells, endothelial cells, and astrocytes was completely abolished in AC mice but robustly reestablished and strengthened by exercise (Figure 6N–P). In summary, our cell–cell communication analysis revealed widespread signaling decoupling in the aged spinal cord microenvironment. Exercise intervention partially reversed these disruptions, primarily by restoring GAP pathway signaling and reestablishing the central regulatory roles of fibroblasts, which may be essential for maintaining and repairing neuroglial homeostasis.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we employed single‐nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA‐seq) to construct a high‐resolution cellular atlas of the mouse spinal cord across different ages and aerobic exercise conditions. Our analysis systematically delineated age‐related alterations in cell‐type composition, lineage trajectory dynamics, regulatory network remodeling, and intercellular communication, and further revealed the potential restorative effects of exercise on these processes. These findings not only enhance our understanding of spinal cord aging at the cellular and molecular levels but also provide mechanistic insights into how exercise may mitigate age‐associated neurodegeneration.

We observed pronounced shifts in the cellular composition within the aging spinal cord. Notably, the proportion of oligodendrocytes was reduced in aged control (AC) mice compared with young controls (YC), suggesting potential impairments in myelination and metabolic support. Interestingly, exercise led to a further reduction in oligodendrocyte proportions in both young (YE) and aged mice (AE). Rather than indicating oligodendrocyte loss, this decline may reflect a relative redistribution of cell lineages, particularly an increase in neurons and astrocytes, forming an optimized cellular ecosystem that supports enhanced neurotrophic and homeostatic functions. Aging was also associated with aberrant increases in microglia, Schwann cells, fibroblasts, and ependymal cells, reflecting enhanced inflammation, fibrosis, and disruption of neuroepithelial homeostasis. These trends are consistent with previous reports of microglial activation and fibrotic expansion in the aging brain and spinal cord [1, 23, 24]. Remarkably, exercise effectively suppressed the excessive expansion of these cell types, restoring their proportions toward youthful levels. This suggests that exercise limits pathological remodeling of the spinal microenvironment and helps maintain cellular ecological balance. Of particular interest, oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) were significantly reduced in aged mice, indicating compromised myelin regeneration and repair capacity. Exercise intervention robustly increased OPC proportions in both young and aged mice, suggesting that exercise helps maintain the OPC pool and thereby enhances the regenerative potential of the spinal cord. These findings align with previous studies showing that physical activity promotes OPC proliferation and myelin plasticity [25, 26].

Pseudotime analyses revealed marked deviations in the differentiation trajectories of glial lineages, including oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, and microglia. These alterations were characterized by misaligned transcriptional activation sequences and disrupted functional module dynamics. For instance, oligodendrocytes exhibited a continuum from early synaptic regulation and glial differentiation to late‐stage membrane remodeling and myelin formation, reflecting the progressive acquisition of mature functions. Astrocytes showed dynamic expression of gene modules related to cytoskeletal reorganization, ion homeostasis, and neurotrophic support, suggesting a staged structural and functional transition. Microglia demonstrated a gradual shift from homeostatic maintenance to inflammatory activation and tissue remodeling, reflecting a transformation from resting to reactive states. These findings highlight that aging not only alters glial cell abundance but also disrupts the spatiotemporal coordination of their lineage‐specific functional programs. Such trajectory reprogramming has not been systematically examined in previous brain region‐focused studies on exercise, and our results suggest that exercise not only modulates cell composition but also restores appropriate transcriptional trajectories at the lineage level.

Using gene regulatory network (GRN) modeling, we identified several key regulators that exhibited reduced centrality and dysregulated expression with aging but partial recovery following exercise. Genes such as Plp1, C4b, and Spp1 showed consistent restoration across differential expression, pseudotemporal dynamics, and network centrality analyses, implying potential roles in mediating exercise‐induced cell fate remodeling. Notably, Plp1 is essential for myelin formation and has been implicated in maintaining myelin integrity and regeneration [27, 28], whereas C4b is recognized as a key mediator of age‐associated synaptic pruning by microglia [29, 30]. In our study, these exercise‐rescued hub genes not only regained expression levels but also reestablished their high‐connectivity roles within GRNs, indicating that exercise can reconfigure the internal regulatory architecture of aging cells. Such centrality‐based inference of molecular mechanisms offers promising targets for future therapeutic strategies.

Our analysis of intercellular communication revealed that aging induced widespread network decoupling within the spinal cord, with both the number and strength of interactions reduced, reflecting impaired cross‐cellular coordination. This fragmentation is consistent with previous observations in the aging brain and retina [31, 32]. Interestingly, certain communication axes were paradoxically enhanced with aging, particularly those involving immune–glial interactions. Fibroblasts exhibited substantial remodeling of their signaling output, including a shift in communication targets, with markedly increased interactions with OPCs and decreased connections with ependymal cells, suggesting functional reprogramming within the aging microenvironment. The neuron–OPC axis displayed fewer but stronger interactions, suggesting a shift from diffuse signaling to focused, high‐intensity crosstalk, potentially reflecting altered neuro–glial coupling demands within local niches.

Exercise partially reversed these aberrant communication patterns. In the AE group, the number of intercellular interactions partially recovered; although overall signaling strength remained lower than in the YC group, the increased frequency of signaling events suggested reactivation of previously dormant or inefficient pathways. Two‐dimensional signaling‐space mapping revealed substantial remodeling of neuron–OPC communication following exercise, supporting the notion that exercise enhances the plasticity of spinal intercellular signaling. At the pathway level, integrated manifold learning and centrality analyses identified the GTPase‐activating protein (GAP) signaling pathway as a key module underlying aging‐ and exercise‐induced remodeling of communication networks. The GAP pathway exhibited the greatest functional similarity shifts with aging, with fibroblasts showing near‐complete loss of sending, receiving, influencing, and mediating capacities within this pathway. Exercise effectively restored these capacities, reestablishing fibroblast‐mediated connections with pericytes, ependymal cells, endothelial cells, and astrocytes. These findings suggest that aging induces systemic collapse of coordinated intercellular networks within the spinal cord, whereas exercise not only rectifies transcriptional programs at the single‐cell level but also restores the connectivity and centrality of critical pathways at the systems level, thereby promoting tissue homeostasis and functional recovery.

Extending from the spinal cord to the broader central nervous system (CNS), numerous studies have demonstrated that exercise elicits convergent neuroprotective and regenerative programs across diverse brain regions [33]. In the hippocampus and corpus callosum, aerobic training promotes OPC proliferation and myelin renewal, while concurrently restoring astrocytic glutamate metabolism and mitochondrial function [26]. Exercise has also been shown to attenuate microglial inflammatory priming and enhance neuro–glial coupling in aged cortical and hippocampal tissues [34]. These findings parallel our observations in the spinal cord, where exercise restored glial lineage coordination, rebalanced intercellular signaling, and enhanced OPC maintenance. Collectively, these observations suggest that shared molecular and cellular programs underlie exercise‐induced rejuvenation throughout the CNS, with the spinal cord emerging as an integral yet previously underexplored component of this network.

Moreover, the Molecular Transducers of Physical Activity Consortium (MoTrPac) has recently generated comprehensive multi‐omics datasets defining systemic molecular responses to exercise across multiple tissues. Although spinal cord tissue has not yet been included in these analyses, MoTrPac identified conserved cross‐tissue molecular networks modulated by exercise, particularly those involved in immune regulation, inflammatory signaling, energy metabolism, and mitochondrial function [11]. The suppression of age‐associated microglial expansion, restoration of intercellular communication, and recovery of mitochondrial‐related pathways observed in our study align closely with these systemic signatures. By delineating the cellular and regulatory architecture of the spinal cord response, our study integrates this critical CNS structure into the expanding framework of exercise biology, thereby bridging systemic and neural perspectives on exercise‐induced rejuvenation and homeostatic maintenance.

sec.title: Limitations of the Study
sec.p: This study focused exclusively on aerobic exercise training, whereas resistance or combined exercise modalities may engage distinct molecular mechanisms and elicit different neural adaptations. In addition, the current findings may be limited by the exercise intensity applied. It remains possible that higher intensity (vigorous) exercise training could produce divergent outcomes, particularly through lactate‐ and PGC‐1α‐related signaling pathways that regulate neurotrophic and metabolic responses (e.g., BDNF, kynurenine, and irisin pathways). Systematic evaluation of intensity‐dependent responses will therefore be essential for fully defining the dose–response relationship between exercise and spinal cord rejuvenation.
